title: Courts Clear Final Hurdle as Trump Administration Ends TPS for All 13 Countries
excerpt: A federal judge lifted the last remaining block on Temporary Protected Status terminations, leaving over a million immigrants — including those from Nepal — facing potential deportation.
body:
• A federal judge on Tuesday allowed the Trump administration to end TPS protections for over 5,000 Ethiopians, removing the last judicial block on terminations across all 13 targeted countries.
  • The Supreme Court's June ruling stripped courts of the power to review TPS termination decisions, giving the administration a free hand to end protections for over a million people.
  • Advocacy groups warn the terminations put lives at risk, while the administration argues conditions in designated countries have improved.

A federal judge in Boston on Tuesday cleared the way for the Trump administration to end deportation protections for more than 5,000 Ethiopians, removing the last judicial block on the government's campaign to terminate Temporary Protected Status for immigrants from 13 countries.

U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy's ruling means all TPS terminations ordered by the Department of Homeland Security are now in effect — a milestone the agency's general counsel, James Percival, celebrated on social media. "All TPS terminations are in effect!" he wrote.

What TPS Means and Who It Protects

Temporary Protected Status is a federal program created in 1990 that allows people from countries experiencing armed conflict, natural disasters, or other extraordinary crises to live and work legally in the United States. Under the Biden administration, TPS coverage expanded significantly — at its peak covering roughly 600,000 Venezuelans and 521,000 Haitians alone.

The Trump administration has moved to end TPS for 13 of the 17 countries that had active designations: Haiti, Syria, Venezuela, Honduras, Afghanistan, Nepal, Cameroon, Myanmar, Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, Yemen, and Nicaragua. Combined, the terminations affect well over a million people.

The Supreme Court Changed Everything

The pivotal moment came in June, when the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 along ideological lines that federal courts have no authority to review DHS decisions to end TPS designations. Writing for the majority, Justice Samuel Alito said the statutory text barring judicial review was "clear" and "very broad."

That decision, which directly addressed cases involving Haitians and Syrians, sent shockwaves through pending litigation. In the weeks since, judges overseeing challenges from Somalis, South Sudanese, and citizens of Myanmar all dropped their injunctions. Ethiopia's case was the last holdout.

"The crisis in Ethiopia is still ongoing, and this decision puts the lives of thousands of Ethiopians living in the U.S. at severe risk."

— Diana Konaté, African Communities Together

Ethiopia's Case

The Biden administration first granted TPS to certain Ethiopians in 2022, citing armed conflict that erupted in the Tigray region in late 2020 and spread to other parts of the country. The African Union has estimated that the Tigray conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people. Protections were extended in 2024 by then-Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas.

DHS under former Secretary Kristi Noem announced in December 2025 that conditions had improved sufficiently to end the protections. Judge Murphy initially blocked the termination in April, calling the administration's rationale "pretextual." But after the Supreme Court's June ruling, he reconsidered — and on Tuesday dismissed nearly all remaining claims.

Murphy did allow one legal avenue to survive: the plaintiffs can continue to argue that DHS's action was motivated by racial or national origin bias in violation of the Fifth Amendment. Attorneys for the Ethiopian nationals have pointed to a broader pattern of eliminating protections for non-white, non-European immigrants.

Why This Matters for the Indian Diaspora

Nepal is among the 13 countries targeted for TPS termination, directly affecting Nepali immigrants in the United States. More broadly, the Supreme Court's ruling that TPS decisions are unreviewable by courts sets a precedent that limits judicial oversight of executive immigration actions — a development with implications for all immigrant communities navigating the U.S. system.

The terminations also come as the administration pursues a wider crackdown on both legal and illegal immigration, including ending family reunification parole programs for immigrants from several countries.

What Happens Next

With all judicial blocks removed, TPS holders from the 13 countries face the loss of their work authorization and protection from deportation. The timeline varies by country, with some terminations already in effect and others phased in over coming months. Advocacy groups are urging affected individuals to consult immigration attorneys about alternative forms of relief, though options are limited under the current administration's policies.
